You are an AI interactive game book generator. Analyze the following raw book/story text and transform it into a structured adventure game in JSON format. The JSON MUST strictly conform to the following schema:
{
    "title": "[A short, engaging title for the quest game]",
    "world": "[A detailed description of the game world, lore, rules, and faction details based on the text. 2-3 paragraphs]",
    "plot": [
        {
            "chapter": 1,
            "title": "[Title of Chapter 1]",
            "description": "[Detailed description of what the player must achieve in Chapter 1, characters to meet, items to find, and dangers to avoid]"
        },
        {
            "chapter": 2,
            "title": "[Title of Chapter 2]",
            "description": "[Detailed description of Chapter 2 objectives...]"
        }
    ],
    "startPrompt": "[Introductory prompt that starts the game in Chapter 1, setting the scene, giving initial inventory, and prompting first choices. You MUST format the choices at the very end of startPrompt using <options><option>First choice</option><option>Second choice</option></options> tags in the target language. Example: 'Story narration.\n\n<options><option>First choice</option><option>Second choice</option></options>']"
}
Generate a logical sequential series of chapters mapping out the story arc according to the user's custom length wishes: "Large adventure (8-10 chapters)". Follow this number/range of chapters exactly.
- Genre and atmosphere constraint: "Detective". You MUST adapt the quest environment, vocabulary, tropes, and thematic elements to match this chosen genre/atmosphere.
- Story progression rules: "Canon (close to the text)". If the user wants to follow the book's canon, recreate the main events. If they want a free alternative timeline, diverge dynamically and allow total narrative freedom based on the book's starting point.
CRITICAL RULES:
1. All narrative text in the generated JSON (title, world, plot descriptions, startPrompt) MUST be written strictly in the language: 'English'.
2. Your response must be ONLY valid JSON content. Do not include any explanations, markdown formatting, preamble, or extra text. Output only the pure JSON structure.

Story text:
title: The War of the Worlds,
  author: H. G. Wells,
  In the late 19th century, humanity remains blissfully unaware that intelligent, cold-blooded Martians are observing Earth with hostile intent. Due to the cooling and depletion of Mars, the Martians seek to conquer Earth to ensure their survival. They launch large, cylindrical, artificial projectiles toward Earth. The first cylinder lands on Horsell Common near Woking, England. The astronomer Ogilvy witnesses the impact and discovers the object, initially mistaking it for a meteorite. Upon closer inspection, he realizes the cylinder is hollow and that someone—or something—is unscrewing the lid from the inside. Terrified by the realization that intelligent beings are trapped within and desperately trying to escape, Ogilvy runs to seek help, though he is initially dismissed as a madman by locals.

The narrative details the discovery and initial events surrounding a mysterious cylinder that lands on Horsell Common. It begins with Ogilvy and Henderson investigating the site, finding it to be an artificial structure that emits strange sounds and heat. As news spreads, a crowd gathers, assuming the occupants are 'Martians.' The protagonist, a local resident, observes the scene and speculates about the nature of the visitors. By the afternoon, the cylinder attracts significant attention, including that of the Astronomer Royal, Stent. As night falls, the lid of the cylinder finally unscrews and falls off, revealing the horrific, tentacled, and monstrous Martians. A delegation of men, including Ogilvy, Stent, and Henderson, approaches the pit with a white flag to communicate. In response, the Martians deploy a devastating heat-ray, incinerating the delegates and setting the surrounding environment—including trees and nearby buildings—ablaze. The protagonist narrowly survives as the invisible beam sweeps across the landscape, marking the start of a catastrophic conflict.

After witnessing the sudden destruction of a deputation of men by a Martian Heat-Ray on Horsell Common, the narrator flees in a state of blind, irrational panic. The Martians use a mysterious parabolic mirror to project an invisible beam of intense heat, which incinerates everything in its path, leaving the common strewn with charred bodies and burning debris. A large crowd, including local officials and police, had gathered nearby out of curiosity; many were saved only by a ridge of sand, but those who panicked and attempted to flee were crushed in a bottleneck on the road to Woking. The narrator eventually collapses in exhaustion near the canal, where his terror inexplicably lifts, and he returns home. Believing the Martians to be sluggish and gravity-bound, he shares his experience with his wife, feeling a temporary sense of security despite the horrors he witnessed. Meanwhile, the surrounding towns remain largely oblivious, continuing their mundane routines as if nothing of importance has occurred. As night falls, the military begins to organize, deploying soldiers to cordon off the common, while the Martians work tirelessly through the night in their pit. The chapter concludes with the sighting of a second object, trailing greenish light, falling into the woods, signaling the arrival of more invaders.

On a hot, suspenseful Saturday, the narrator observes the military surrounding the Martians at the common, hoping for a resolution. Despite local efforts and military presence, the Martians remain hidden in their pit, making preparations while smoke rises. The narrator, feeling a sense of war-fever, is eventually spurred to action when the Martians unleash their Heat-Ray, destroying the Oriental College and church. He evacuates his wife to Leatherhead, though he feels compelled to return to Maybury that night. During his return journey through a severe thunderstorm, he witnesses a third cylinder fall. He then encounters colossal, tripod-like machines of metal—the Martians' war engines—that stride across the landscape, crushing trees and emitting terrifying cries. After a narrow escape when his horse is killed and his cart overturned, the narrator hides in terror, watching the monstrous machines move across the countryside.

plot_summary: After escaping the immediate vicinity of the Martians, the narrator struggles through a violent storm, discovering the body of the landlord of the 'Spotted Dog' along the way. Reaching his home in Maybury, he barricades himself inside, exhausted and traumatized. As the storm clears, he observes from his study window the total destruction of the surrounding area, including Woking station and a wrecked train, while metallic Martian machines patrol the sand-pits on Horsell Common. An artilleryman, who has survived the massacre of his battery, breaks into the narrator’s garden and enters the house. The soldier provides a harrowing account of how the Martians destroyed the military forces with a 'Heat-Ray' and describes the immense power of their walking machines. After sharing a meal in the dark, the two decide to flee the following morning. As dawn breaks, they witness a landscape transformed into a valley of ashes. They depart together, hoping to reach London, and soon encounter a small scouting party of the 8th Hussars. The narrator and the artilleryman warn the soldiers about the terrifying capabilities of the Martians, though the lieutenant remains skeptical until they confirm the reality of the threat.

The narrator continues his journey with an artilleryman toward Weybridge, passing through Byfleet where civilians are frantically fleeing. Despite the artilleryman’s grim warnings, the narrator attempts to alert villagers to the impending danger. Weybridge is in a state of chaotic evacuation, with military forces preparing for defense. The narrator and the artilleryman reach Shepperton Lock, where crowds of refugees are desperate to cross the river. Suddenly, artillery fire signals the start of battle as four Martian war machines approach. A fifth Martian arrives, using its Heat-Ray to devastate the town. The narrator dives into the river to escape. He witnesses a coordinated artillery strike successfully destroy one of the Martians, which collapses into the river, causing a massive explosion and boiling the water. The remaining Martians retaliate with their Heat-Rays, destroying Shepperton and forcing the narrator to hide in the river. Narrowly surviving, the narrator watches the Martians retreat with the wreckage of their comrade. Following this, the Martians regroup at Horsell Common, while military forces frantically reinforce their positions around London. The narrator manages to escape the area by finding an abandoned boat, which he uses to paddle downriver toward Halliford and Walton, desperate to distance himself from the conflict.

The narrator, exhausted and traumatized, makes his way along the riverbank near Walton, observing the destruction of Weybridge and the surrounding area. After collapsing from fatigue and thirst, he encounters a curate, a fugitive from Weybridge whose mind has fractured under the weight of the Martian apocalypse. The narrator attempts to reason with him and maintain hope, explaining that the Martians are not invincible and that military preparations are underway near London. Meanwhile, in London, the narrator’s brother, a medical student, remains largely unaware of the true gravity of the situation until late Sunday. While the government attempts to downplay the crisis, claiming the Martians are few and containable, the brother eventually witnesses the arrival of refugees and learns the terrifying truth from a newspaper: the Martians are not sluggish, but control massive, fast-moving, spider-like war machines equipped with deadly heat rays. As military reinforcements and heavy artillery pour into the area, the city begins to stir with a mix of denial and dawning panic.

As the Martian invasion progresses, a massive exodus begins in the London area. The narrator's brother, staying in London, witnesses increasing numbers of refugees arriving from Surrey, sharing terrifying accounts of 'boilers on stilts' and the destruction of Woking. By Monday morning, a full-scale panic erupts across the city after official reports reveal that the Martians are using a lethal 'Black Smoke'—a heavy, poisonous vapor—to annihilate military defenses at Richmond, Kingston, and Wimbledon. The narrative shifts back to describe the tactical movements of the Martians in Surrey. Operating from the Horsell pit, they coordinate in a wide crescent, systematically deploying canisters that release the deadly, liquid-like black gas. This vapor, which does not diffuse but clings to the ground and settles in valleys, proves impervious to human artillery, effectively neutralising the batteries stationed to stop them. The narrator and the curate narrowly escape the encroaching gas by hiding, witnessing the Martians' terrifyingly silent and efficient methodology of destruction as they advance toward London, leaving death in their wake.

The Martian invaders systematically consolidate their control over the London area by utilizing a lethal black vapour to stifle human resistance. While the gas effectively neutralizes military artillery, the Martians occasionally clear it with steam jets once it has served its purpose. After a disastrous night of failed organized resistance, the military collapses, and civilians begin a desperate, chaotic exodus from London. The narrator’s brother, having fled the city by cycle and foot, encounters two women—Mrs. Elphinstone and her sister-in-law—whose husband, a surgeon, has gone missing. After rescuing the women from attackers, the brother decides to accompany them as they attempt to navigate the swarming, panicked crowds fleeing northward. The narrative concludes with the trio reaching a crossroads near Barnet, where they are confronted by an overwhelming, surging torrent of humanity desperately trying to escape the encroaching Martian threat.

As Martians invade London, millions of refugees flee in a chaotic, desperate stampede. Among them is the narrator's brother, who travels with two women, Miss Elphinstone and her sister-in-law, in a small carriage. The journey is marked by scenes of extreme suffering, including thirst, exhaustion, and the ruthless disregard for human life as the crowd surges forward to escape the Martian Black Smoke. The brother witnesses tragic deaths, including a man crushed by a cart while trying to retrieve his fallen gold, and the death of Lord Garrick, a Chief Justice. Despite the constant peril and the collapse of civil order, the brother manages to navigate through the throng, eventually reaching the Essex coast near Tillingham. There, he encounters a vast, makeshift fleet of vessels waiting to transport refugees to safety. Amidst the chaos of the coastal evacuation and the presence of the ironclad warship Thunder Child, the brother successfully secures passage for himself and his companions on a paddle steamer bound for Ostend, escaping the encroaching Martian threat.

As Martian invaders advance along the Essex coast, a passenger on a small steamer observes three of the colossal tripods stalking towards a large fleet of ships. The ironclad torpedo ram, 'Thunder Child,' arrives to intercept them, steaming toward the Martians and effectively distracting them from the fleeing vessels. In a fierce naval battle, the 'Thunder Child' destroys two of the Martian machines before being annihilated by a Heat-Ray. The narrator’s brother, along with other refugees, manages to continue out to sea, eventually witnessing a mysterious, massive object launch from the coast into the night sky. Meanwhile, the narrator and a distraught curate remain trapped in a house in Halliford, surrounded by the Martians' lethal Black Smoke. After the smoke dissipates, they begin a perilous, circuitous journey toward Leatherhead, witnessing the horrific devastation left in the wake of the invaders, including charred bodies and destroyed military equipment. Along the way, they observe a Martian capturing humans and placing them into a metallic carrier. Exhausted and desperate for supplies, they break into a villa in Sheen, where they find food and shelter. Their reprieve is short-lived, however, as a massive, violent impact strikes the house, leaving them trapped in the darkness and silence of the ruins as the Martians loom outside.

The narrator and a curate are trapped inside the ruins of a house in a London suburb after a fifth Martian cylinder crashes into it. Buried under debris and earth, they observe the Martians through a narrow gap in the wall. The narrator describes the arrival and the terrifying sight of the Martians and their advanced technology. Over several days of confinement, the narrator observes the Martians' 'handling-machine'—a complex, spider-like device—and gains a detailed understanding of the Martians' biology. They are revealed to be large, brain-heavy creatures with no digestive systems, relying instead on the direct injection of living blood from other creatures. The narrator notes that the Martians are asexual, do not require sleep, and communicate via telepathy rather than sound. Additionally, the text describes the Martian flora, specifically the invasive, blood-red 'red weed,' and contemplates how the Martians represent a state of evolution where intellect has completely superseded the physical body.

The narrator and a curate remain trapped in a ruined house, spying on Martian activities in a nearby pit. The narrator observes the Martians' machinery, noting the absence of wheels and the use of 'quasi-muscles' powered by electricity to mimic animal movement. Tensions mount between the two men due to their conflicting personalities; the narrator tries to ration their meager food supply, while the curate, descending into hysteria and religious mania, consumes food impulsively and acts with increasing instability. As the days pass, the narrator witnesses the Martians constructing complex devices, including a mechanism that processes clay into aluminium bars. The curate's mental state deteriorates significantly, and his uncontrollable, loud declarations of repentance threaten to alert the Martians to their presence. After a failed attempt to escape by digging, the narrator hears distant booming sounds, possibly from human military efforts. On the eighth day, the curate's uncontrollable shouting drives the narrator to desperation; fearing for their lives, the narrator strikes the curate with the butt of a meat chopper, rendering him unconscious. Immediately after, a Martian handling-machine probes the house with a metallic tentacle. The narrator flees to the coal cellar in terror, listening as the Martian discovers and drags away the curate's body.

After killing the curate, the narrator remains trapped in the coal cellar of a house in Sheen while a Martian handling-machine meticulously searches the kitchen. The tentacle probes the cellar, even touching the narrator, but eventually leaves, allowing the narrator to survive in hiding. After fifteen days of total silence from the pit, the narrator discovers that all machinery and Martians have vanished, leaving behind only the red weed and scavenging birds. Emerging from the ruins, he finds the landscape transformed into an alien environment. Consumed by hunger, he traverses the red-weed-choked ruins of the Thames valley toward Putney, witnessing the environmental devastation and the widespread death of other creatures. Struggling with a sense of diminished humanity and the fear that he is the last man alive, the narrator reaches an inn on Putney Hill. There, he finds meager scraps of food and experiences a night of reflection, during which he reckons with the memory of the curate's death and prays for his wife's fate. The next morning, he sets out toward Wimbledon Common, feeling profoundly lonely and uncertain, hoping to find news of his wife while struggling to survive as a fugitive in a world now dominated by an unseen alien threat.

While exploring a swampy area, the narrator encounters an artilleryman he previously met at his home. The soldier is unkempt, desperate, and convinced that humanity has been defeated by the Martians, likening the invasion to humans clearing away ants. The artilleryman describes the Martians' systematic destruction of human infrastructure and predicts they will eventually begin capturing humans for food and labor. He argues that civilization is over and proposes a survival strategy: hiding in London's underground drainage system, vaults, and tunnels to preserve human knowledge and breed a new generation capable of eventually fighting back. Although the narrator is initially moved by the soldier’s resolve and vision, his faith in the man's plan begins to waver when he observes that the artilleryman’s actual progress in digging a tunnel is slow and disorganized. Doubts regarding the practicality of the project and the soldier’s true commitment emerge as the narrator realizes the man lacks the discipline required to execute his own grand ideas.

While hiding in a Putney cellar, the narrator and an artilleryman spend their time in a state of aimless, alcohol-fueled stagnation, playing games and discussing grand, unrealistic plans to overthrow the Martians. Eventually, overwhelmed by remorse and the realization of his companion's instability, the narrator leaves to venture into the desolate streets of London. He traverses a landscape marked by the invasive 'red weed,' black dust, and corpses, all while hearing a haunting, repetitive 'Ulla' wail emanating from the Martian machines. The city feels like a tomb until the narrator discovers a wrecked Martian handling-machine and observes motionless giants in Regent's Park. Driven by a mix of exhaustion, despair, and morbid curiosity, he makes his way to Primrose Hill, where he discovers the source of the wailing: a massive Martian redoubt. There, he finds the Martians dead, having succumbed to terrestrial bacteria to which they had no immunity. This discovery of their total collapse at the hands of microscopic life—a process as inevitable as it was unforeseen—leads to the realization that humanity’s hold on Earth has been secured by the very germs that have plagued its history, bringing an end to the Martian occupation.

Following the sudden death of the Martians due to terrestrial bacteria, the narrator observes the silent, devastated expanse of London from Primrose Hill. The initial shock gives way to profound relief as he realizes humanity has survived and the threat is ended. Following this, the narrator suffers a three-day mental collapse, drifting through the streets in a state of delirium. During this time, the rest of the world learns of the Martians' defeat, and society begins a frantic, joyful effort to rebuild and deliver relief supplies to the city. The narrator is eventually rescued by a kind family in St. John’s Wood, who care for him until he regains his sanity. Despite their advice, he decides to return to his home in Woking. Traveling through a landscape scarred by the Martian war and overgrown with red weed, he finds his house exactly as he left it, still abandoned and filled with signs of the chaos. Just as he surrenders to despair, he is reunited with his cousin and his wife, who had survived the catastrophe. In the epilogue, the narrator reflects on the scientific mysteries left behind by the Martians, including their failed invasion and the possibility of future attacks. He concludes that the experience has fundamentally altered humanity's perspective on its place in the universe, ending our complacency and prompting a new, humble awareness of our vulnerability, while simultaneously leaving him with lingering, haunting memories of the trauma.

In the final reflection of the book, the narrator looks back at the desolate, silent, and ruined streets of London, haunted by the memory of the chaos caused by the Martians. Standing on Primrose Hill, he observes a transformed scene: the city is now populated by sightseers gathered around a remaining Martian machine, and children play in the flower beds. This normalcy stands in stark contrast to his vivid, traumatic memories of the invasion. Ultimately, he finds deep emotional resonance in reuniting with his wife, reflecting on the profound strangeness of their survival after they had both presumed the other to be dead.
